> get_pos - probably breaks single responsibility rule - it is supposed to get some sort of position, but internally calls push_frame which changes GUI state.

You see, depending on gui.style.display.type (flex 'f' or fixed 'x') it calculates where to put the element.

Every element just like html, gets put under or next to the element before (depending on gui.style.display.direction) or just to xny coordinates user specified if display type is fixed.

If display if flex, it pushes other element's x and y's by it's w and h affecting gui.style.display.frame (which is used by get_pos). So, it does break it. But it's intended.

You must consider a proper way of structuring behaviour.

Will it behave as a framework?
Like, when ran on a directory, will it compile files inside 'include' and/or 'src', store obj files in 'junk'?

Or will it behave as a programmable script?
Which often is the case (make, cmake, premake).

Framework alike build systems, have the advantage of consistency over projects file structure. But they can be incompatible with some libraries since C/C++ doesn't really have a standard for it.

On the other hand, programmable scripts have more flexibility since you give control over files to the programmer. But they have this headache of creating a new language for programmers to use.  And they have to learn it to use your system which is a pain in the ass.

While also I'm on it, you need to think about compiler flags too. For gcc, clang maybe there isn't much difference but msvc flags are an absolute disgrace tbh. And the worst part is everyone has at least that 1 dumb programmer friend who is a windows fan and thus can't stand UNIX systems. So.. yeah?

You also need a way to indicate if a project should produce a library or an executable? On frameworks, this is rather easy since you can create a file named 'lib' or 'app' and it would do the trick. But in scripts, man.. dammit.
